sources.news_title: Democratic Win Set to Reshuffle U.S. Energy Policy
sources.text:
The blue wave in the midterm elections that will put Democrats in charge of the House and Senate could reshape U.S. energy policies.
Democrats in charge of both chambers of Congress and its key committees, Democratic governors in key data-center development states such as Ohio, Georgia, and Texas, a Democrat in Georgia’s utilities regulator, and the first Democratic member of the Texas oil regulator since 1990 would seek to stymie the Trump Administration’s pro-fossil fuel and unchecked data center expansion.
Investigations into oil deals involving the White House, including “the biggest oil deal in world history” in Venezuela, and the ‘diesel deal’ with Russia’s Vladimir Putin on the eve of the elections are likely to be top of the agenda.
Policy uncertainty at the federal level will increase, as Democrats are likely to attempt to bring back some clean energy tax credits. President Donald Trump has vowed to become ‘Mr Veto’ and veto legislation he doesn’t like.
The Democratic-majority Congress will need support from Republican lawmakers to overcome a presidential veto, so changes to the energy policy are unlikely to be radical, but rather a compromise. Related: The Iran War Isn't Over, but Oil Traders Are Already Pricing In Peace
Executive orders and war powers remain a tool for President Trump, but Congress now controls appropriations and budgets, so both sides will have to make concessions – “deals” in Trump’s parlance – in many key policy areas, including energy.
A Democratic-controlled Congress could push for regulation of AI, while governors from Texas to Ohio could halt the expansion plans amid concerns about how soaring power demand from AI would hit household bills. No wonder tech stocks crashed on Wednesday as most results of the midterm elections showed stunning victories in many key-race states.
Investigations are coming, Democratic Senator Ed of Massachusetts said on election night.
“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” said Markey, who is on the environment and public works committee.
In Texas, oil and gas engineer Jon Rosenthal won the open seat on the three-member Texas Railroad Commission, becoming the first Democrat on the commission since 1990. Rosenthal will be in the minority, but could influence some issues, including data center permitting and wastewater disposal from oil and gas production.
The war in Iran is the biggest international issue that Congress will face, and that will influence international oil prices and U.S. fuel prices in the coming months.
Analysts still believe there is currently more chance of a U.S. escalation rather than de-escalation in Iran, but the Democratic Congress, as of January 1, could pressure Trump into reaching a deal.
“With war funding and appointees now subject to a hostile majority, the administration faces greater institutional pressure to pursue a Hormuz deal rather than a further round of strikes,” analysts at Rystad Energy said on the day after the elections.
“A restoration of flows through the Strait of Hormuz is the prerequisite for Middle East crude supply and refined product inventories to normalize,” they noted.
U.S. voters showed that the cost of living and the cost of gasoline top their concerns and punished the Administration, whose war on Iran drove fuel prices to record highs for this time of year.
The first sign of whether compromises between the executive and legislative branches could work will be seen as early as November 9, when a proposed bipartisan permitting bill is scheduled for a procedural vote in the Senate.
Both the oil and clean energy industries support expediting reform to build America’s energy infrastructure. But the sweeping win could embolden the most progressive Democrat lawmakers to seek bargains in texts in the bill they argue would favor the oil and gas industry over renewable energy.
Analysts at TD Cowen have now lowered the odds of the bill passing Congress to about 25%, from a 40% chance before the election
Wood Mackenzie analysts, however, said that “permitting reform has a path that other Democratic priorities do not.”
By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

sources.news_title: Democrats Push Clean Energy Plan to Cut Bills and Counter Trump’s Fossil Fuel Agenda
sources.text:
Some Democrats say they will pursue expanded clean-energy policies to help bring down rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, even as President Donald Trump vows to use his veto power aggressively.
With new majorities in the House and Senate following last week’s midterm elections, Democrats will be able to shape an agenda focused on clean energy and climate change. Although those issues have traditionally been central to the party, climate policy was not a major focus of this election cycle.
Democrats can launch investigations and hearings into the Republican administration’s rollback of climate policies and cancellation of clean-energy grants. They may also seek to reverse some of those changes and restore incentives for renewable energy.
Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, said Trump’s attacks on clean energy had increased costs for taxpayers. Democrats, he said, will “work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”
Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, said people working to develop clean energy “feel bolstered” by the election results.
Major legislative changes would require Republican backing because Democrats will not have enough votes to override presidential vetoes. Even with bipartisan support, however, cheaper energy is not guaranteed. Prices are also shaped by fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.
“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”
Trump has veto power but believes he and Democrats can find common ground
After Tuesday’s election, Trump said Democrats would send him “things that are insane” and that he would veto them, speaking broadly about potential legislation. In comments to Fox News, however, he predicted that after “a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats would find opportunities to work together.
The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is “committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”
Trump campaigned on lowering energy prices. Instead, his conflict with Iran and other policies pushed up the cost of gasoline, diesel and electricity. His administration has also canceled numerous clean-energy projects and grants while slowing the approval process for new clean-energy developments.
Trump has been especially critical of offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a major wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has begun commercial operations.
Former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff, said a shift in Trump’s position on green energy is unlikely.
“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.
Trump favors expanding oil, natural gas and coal production, all of which contribute to climate change, arguing that greater fossil-fuel output would give the United States the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s leading lobbying group, said the change in Washington’s political balance made “the affordability message unmistakable.”
Sommers said in a statement that bipartisan cooperation could reduce costs and strengthen the economy, beginning with an energy-permitting reform proposal unveiled in September. The measure would shorten the time required to begin large energy projects.
Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should oppose the proposal and use their stronger position to advance legislation that expands the clean-energy infrastructure the country needs.
Reversing Trump’s anti-climate policies
The administration has overhauled the Environmental Protection Agency as it promotes fossil fuels and rolls back pollution limits.
Tim Moore, an energy-transition analyst at Clear Street, expects Democrats to investigate the administration’s climate and environmental rollbacks in an effort to prevent some of them from taking effect. They could also seek to amend the Clean Air Act to reduce carbon pollution and oppose cuts to the EPA’s budget, he said.
Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously hopeful that some Republicans will try to distinguish themselves from Trump and support environmental policies. Without Republican votes, however, Democrats’ most ambitious legislation will largely serve as a blueprint for their agenda in 2028, he said.
Climate policy is not necessarily at the top of the Democrats’ priority list. The party is also focused on health care access, trade tariffs and the war in Iran.
Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should emphasize health care, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulation of Big Tech.
A possible stalemate on clean energy and climate policy
David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, expects divided government to produce a federal stalemate on much of climate and energy policy. He said bipartisan agreement could still emerge on measures such as permitting reform.
Victor expects Democratic investigations and hearings to focus on corruption and other issues that may only indirectly involve energy and climate. Like Casten, he said many Democratic bills are unlikely to become law but could define what the party would pursue if it wins the White House in 2028.
“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”
The administration’s conduct is one of the biggest unknowns, Victor said. It could use executive authority to intensify its rollback of climate and environmental regulations.
States could advance clean energy without waiting for Congress
Democrats won gubernatorial races in states that have long been controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.
Leah Stokes, a political scientist at UC Santa Barbara, said those victories could lead to significant state-level climate action next year. Climate leadership has traditionally emerged from the states, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic that clean-energy tax credits could be extended because some Republicans support them.
Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects clean-energy momentum to grow in states that elected Democratic governors, especially where Democrats also won control of state legislatures.
“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”
___
Associated Press writers Alexa St. John and Matthew Daly contributed to this report.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.
“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”
___
Associated Press writers Alexa St. John and Matthew Daly contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Democrats plan to push clean energy to lower bills and challenge Trump’s fossil fuel agenda
sources.text:
Democrats plan to push clean energy to lower bills and challenge Trump’s fossil fuel agenda
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.
With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week's midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.
Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.
Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will "work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”
American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”
Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.
“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”
Trump said after Tuesday's election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.
The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is "committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”
Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.
Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.
Will the president change his tune on green energy? That's doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.
“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.
Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”
Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The legislation is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.
Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.
The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.
Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.
Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.
Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats' list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.
Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.
David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.
Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.
“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”
One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.
Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.
Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.
Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.
“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”
___
